questions.question: Which description best characterizes supervised fine-tuning on preferred completions (behavior cloning) for aligning a language model to preferences?
questions.choice_A: It directly trains the model to imitate human-approved outputs by maximizing likelihood of those completions.
questions.choice_B: It trains a separate reward model and then optimizes the policy against that reward via reinforcement learning.
questions.choice_C: It selects the best completion from a pool at test time without changing model parameters.
questions.choice_D: It penalizes the probability of all tokens not present in the preferred completion.

questions.question: What is the core idea behind unlikelihood training in preference alignment?
questions.choice_A: Reducing model entropy so it becomes more deterministic.
questions.choice_B: Penalizing the model when it assigns non-negligible probability to explicitly undesired tokens or sequences.
questions.choice_C: Replacing maximum likelihood with a purely adversarial objective.
questions.choice_D: Maximizing the margin between the log-likelihood of preferred and dispreferred samples without any penalty term.

questions.question: In pairwise preference learning with a cross-entropy or logistic loss, what is typically being learned?
questions.choice_A: A mapping from prompts directly to final scores using mean squared error.
questions.choice_B: A generative model that copies the preferred sample exactly.
questions.choice_C: A scoring function over completions such that preferred samples have higher scores than dispreferred ones.
questions.choice_D: A classifier that predicts whether a prompt has any acceptable completion.

questions.question: Which statement about best-of-N selection is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: It requires retraining the model to sample N times per prompt.
questions.choice_B: It is a purely test-time strategy that draws multiple candidates and selects the best under a selection rule.
questions.choice_C: It cannot be combined with any learned preference model.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees the globally optimal completion as N grows.

questions.question: A key practical advantage of behavior cloning on preferred completions compared to RL-based preference optimization is:
questions.choice_A: Lower implementation complexity and often greater training stability.
questions.choice_B: It does not require any labeled data.
questions.choice_C: It guarantees perfect alignment to human preferences.
questions.choice_D: It eliminates exposure bias entirely.

questions.question: Which limitation is most associated with behavior cloning on preferred completions?
questions.choice_A: It cannot scale to large datasets.
questions.choice_B: It often overfits the prompt distribution and struggles with generalization to unseen inputs.
questions.choice_C: It requires on-policy rollouts with learned rewards.
questions.choice_D: It necessarily reduces perplexity on all domains.

questions.question: How does unlikelihood training typically interact with maximum likelihood training in practice?
questions.choice_A: It completely replaces maximum likelihood to avoid instability.
questions.choice_B: It is usually combined with maximum likelihood, adding penalties for bad tokens alongside rewards for good ones.
questions.choice_C: It is used only during evaluation and never during training.
questions.choice_D: It is applied exclusively at the character level rather than token level.

questions.question: What is a common way to construct pairwise preference data for a cross-entropy loss?
questions.choice_A: Randomly pairing any two completions regardless of quality.
questions.choice_B: Pairing a human-preferred completion with a dispreferred one for the same prompt.
questions.choice_C: Pairing completions from different prompts to increase diversity.
questions.choice_D: Pairing completions from the same model but with identical quality ratings.

questions.question: Which selection rule for best-of-N is most compatible with a learned preference model?
questions.choice_A: Select the longest completion because longer outputs contain more information.
questions.choice_B: Select the completion with the highest conditional log-likelihood under the base model.
questions.choice_C: Select the completion with the highest score under the learned preference scorer.
questions.choice_D: Select randomly to avoid bias.

questions.question: Which tradeoff best characterizes best-of-N selection at test time?
questions.choice_A: It reduces latency but increases memory usage.
questions.choice_B: It improves sample quality but increases compute and latency due to multiple generations.
questions.choice_C: It reduces variance by deterministically selecting the first sample.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees lower toxicity regardless of N.

questions.question: Why might unlikelihood training be preferred when the set of undesired behaviors can be enumerated or detected?
questions.choice_A: It allows fine-grained penalties that directly target those behaviors without requiring a full reward model.
questions.choice_B: It eliminates the need for human feedback entirely.
questions.choice_C: It guarantees that the model will never produce those behaviors.
questions.choice_D: It requires less data than maximum likelihood training in all cases.

questions.question: What is a potential failure mode when using only pairwise preference training with a static data distribution?
questions.choice_A: The model may develop a degenerate length prior due to mode dropping.
questions.choice_B: The model may exploit spurious correlations in the preference data and fail to generalize out-of-distribution.
questions.choice_C: The model will necessarily collapse to a single token output.
questions.choice_D: The training becomes unsupervised and loses any guidance from preferences.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the compute vs. data tradeoff in behavior cloning vs. best-of-N?
questions.choice_A: Behavior cloning needs more test-time compute, while best-of-N needs more training data.
questions.choice_B: Behavior cloning shifts cost to training by learning to produce preferred completions, while best-of-N shifts cost to inference by generating multiple candidates.
questions.choice_C: Both approaches have identical compute profiles at training and inference.
questions.choice_D: Best-of-N reduces both training and inference costs simultaneously.

questions.question: When using unlikelihood losses to penalize unsafe content, what is a key stability consideration?
questions.choice_A: Ensuring that the penalties are unbounded to drive probabilities to zero quickly.
questions.choice_B: Calibrating penalty weights so the model does not over-suppress benign tokens that correlate with unsafe content.
questions.choice_C: Applying penalties at every token regardless of context to keep training simple.
questions.choice_D: Disabling maximum likelihood to avoid conflicts with the penalties.

questions.question: Pairwise cross-entropy preference training typically optimizes a logistic objective of the form P(preferred > dispreferred). What is an advantage of this formulation?
questions.choice_A: It provides an absolute scale for quality across prompts.
questions.choice_B: It is invariant to additive shifts in the scoring function, focusing on relative ordering.
questions.choice_C: It enables exact Bayesian inference over human preferences.
questions.choice_D: It removes the need for regularization entirely.

questions.question: Which scenario favors using best-of-N selection without additional training?
questions.choice_A: A setting with stringent latency constraints and limited compute.
questions.choice_B: A setting where model updates are frozen but higher-quality outputs are needed using extra inference compute.
questions.choice_C: A setting where training data is abundant but inference compute is scarce.
questions.choice_D: A setting requiring strict determinism in outputs.

questions.question: What is a common risk when relying exclusively on behavior cloning from curated, preferred completions?
questions.choice_A: Reward hacking due to optimization pressure on a learned reward model.
questions.choice_B: Distributional shift and exposure bias because the model learns only from gold trajectories.
questions.choice_C: Inability to learn long-range dependencies due to the loss function itself.
questions.choice_D: Inherent non-convexity causing guaranteed divergence.

questions.question: How can unlikelihood training be extended from token-level to sequence-level undesired behaviors?
questions.choice_A: By penalizing any token that appears frequently in the corpus.
questions.choice_B: By defining detectors or rules that flag entire spans or patterns, and applying penalties to those spans’ probabilities.
questions.choice_C: By decreasing the learning rate only when undesired tokens occur.
questions.choice_D: By augmenting prompts with negative examples during evaluation.

questions.question: Which hybrid strategy combines training and inference to leverage preferences efficiently?
questions.choice_A: Train with pairwise preference loss to learn a scorer, then use it for best-of-N reranking at test time.
questions.choice_B: Train only with maximum likelihood and sample randomly at test time.
questions.choice_C: Use unlikelihood loss only at test time to reweight samples.
questions.choice_D: Avoid any preference data and rely on temperature tuning.

questions.question: What is a practical consideration when choosing N for best-of-N selection in production?
questions.choice_A: N should be as large as possible because quality always scales linearly with N.
questions.choice_B: N should be chosen to balance marginal quality gains against added latency and cost, which typically exhibit diminishing returns.
questions.choice_C: N must equal the number of tokens in the prompt to be effective.
questions.choice_D: N should be set to 1 to avoid any selection bias.

questions.question: Compared to reinforcement-learning-based preference optimization, what is a distinctive limitation of pairwise cross-entropy preference training when used alone?
questions.choice_A: It cannot model relative preferences across samples.
questions.choice_B: It lacks on-policy data collection, so it may not adapt to the model’s current failure modes without iterative data refresh.
questions.choice_C: It requires higher variance gradient estimators.
questions.choice_D: It cannot be combined with behavior cloning signals.
